---
title: "Span — Which Points Can Your Arrows Reach?"
description: "An original mathematical walkthrough with one running example, concrete numbers and a proof."
---

## Ask a simple question

If you can walk only along arrows (1,0) and (0,1), where can you go? What if both arrows point along the same line?

## Build the intuition

The span of given vectors is the set of all linear combinations of those vectors. It describes the reachable set of positions.

## Write the mathematical relationship

$$
\operatorname{span}\{\mathbf u,\mathbf v\}=\{a\mathbf u+b\mathbf v:a,b\in\mathbb R\}
$$

**Every symbol explained:** span names all linear combinations; u,v are starting vectors; a,b are arbitrary real coefficients; ℝ means real numbers. The colon means 'such that'.

**Substitute real numbers:** With u=(1,0), v=(0,1), choose a=3,b=2 to reach (3,2). With u=(1,0), v=(2,0), every combination has vertical coordinate 0, so you cannot reach (3,2).

## Why the relationship is true

Nonparallel vectors in the plane generate two independent directions and span the plane. Parallel vectors only span a line.

## Where the shortcut stops working

The span always contains the zero vector (choose both coefficients zero); a translated line not through zero is not itself a vector subspace.

## Your turn

Can u=(1,1) and v=(2,2) produce (0,1)? Explain without guessing.

**Source structure:** Ivan Savov, *No Bullshit Guide to Linear Algebra*, second edition, Geometric aspects, §§4.1, 4.4. This is an independently written explanation based on the uploaded **extended preview**, not a transcription of the commercial full book.
